title: Episode 302: Edward II: Piers Gaveston, the Disaster of Bannockburn, and the Fall at Berkeley Castle
description:
The poignant, disastrous, and brutal life of King Edward II: the son of the fierce Edward Longshanks whose twenty-year reign unraveled his father's empire and culminated in England's first formal parliamentary deposition of a monarch. Uninterested in warfare and military glory, Edward preferred rowing, digging ditches, and theatrical masques, lavishing obsessive affection upon his charismatic Gascon favorite, Piers Gaveston. Provoking furious baronial rebellions led by Thomas of Lancaster, Edward watched Gaveston be executed in 1212. Humiliated by Robert the Bruce at the catastrophic Battle of Bannockburn in 1314 and dominated by his corrupt new favorites, the Despensers, Edward was overthrown by his own estranged queen, Isabella 'the She-Wolf of France', and her lover Roger Mortimer. Dying mysteriously in the dark dungeons of Berkeley Castle, discover the tragic story of Edward II.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the tragic, sensitive, and ill-fated sovereign whose reign collapsed under the weight of unrequited expectations, leading to a humiliating defeat at Bannockburn and the first violent deposition of an anointed English king. Here is George with the extraordinary story of Edward II.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: IN THE SHADOW OF LONGSHANKS: 1284 TO 1307
Born in April 1284 at the newly constructed fortress of Caernarfon in Wales, Edward of Caernarfon was the fourth and only surviving son of Edward I and Eleanor of Castile. Handsome, tall, with broad shoulders and athletic physical grace, young Edward was an emotional disappointment to his ferocious father: where Longshanks was consumed by warfare, law, and conquest, young Edward hated tournaments, preferred the companionship of common craftsmen, and enjoyed music, acting, thatching roofs, and rowing boats. In 1300, his father assigned a witty, flamboyant young Gascon knight named Piers Gaveston to the prince's household. The bond between Edward and Gaveston was instant, all-consuming, and passionate: chroniclers described their love as 'beyond the measure of women'. When Prince Edward demanded that his father grant Gaveston the hereditary county of Ponthieu, old King Edward flew into an apoplectic fury, tearing out handfuls of his son's hair and exiling Gaveston from the realm under pain of death.  Growing up as the surviving son of the terrifying, towering Edward Longshanks was an emotional nightmare for young Prince Edward: where his father was an iron-willed conqueror who spent his life in chainmail, young Edward was an artistic, sensitive soul who preferred digging ditches with laborers, breeding horses, practicing carpentry, and swimming in the Thames. His passionate relationship with Piers Gaveston, a dashing, athletic Gascon knight who possessed supreme skill in the tournament lists, was the defining emotional sanctuary of Edward's life. When old King Edward discovered that Prince Edward had gifted Gaveston royal crown lands, the ferocious old monarch attacked his son in a volcanic rage, tearing out clumps of the prince's hair and banishing Gaveston to France under oath of death, driving a permanent wedge between father and son.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE CORONATION AND THE INSOLENCE OF PIERS GAVESTON: 1307 TO 1311
The moment old Longshanks died in July 1307, twenty-three-year-old Edward II immediately recalled Gaveston from exile, bestowing upon him the prestigious Earldom of Cornwall—a title traditionally reserved exclusively for royal princes—and appointing him Regent of England while Edward sailed to France to marry twelve-year-old Princess Isabella, daughter of King Philip IV. At their lavish coronation at Westminster in February 1308, Edward scandalized his French in-laws and the English aristocracy: Edward ignored his beautiful child-bride Isabella, spending the entire feast seated beside Gaveston, who was clad in magnificent royal imperial purple silk adorned with pearls. Gaveston was brilliant, arrogant, and reckless, openly insulting the great English earls with cutting nicknames: calling the King's cousin, the Earl of Lancaster, 'the Churl' and the Earl of Pembroke 'Joseph the Jew'. The furious barons formed a league, issuing the Ordinances of 1311 to restrict royal power and banish Gaveston forever.  The lavish coronation of Edward II and twelve-year-old Princess Isabella of France at Westminster in February 1308 was a diplomatic and aristocratic catastrophe: King Edward spent the entire feast gazing passionately at Piers Gaveston, who wore magnificent royal purple robes stitched with pearls, completely ignoring his French child-bride. Isabella's uncles, the Duke of Burgundy and Count of Evreux, stormed out of the banquet hall in furious disgust, while the English earls seethed with rage at Gaveston's insolent arrogance. Gaveston mocked the great magnates with cruel, witty nicknames: calling Thomas of Lancaster 'the Churl' and 'the Old Hog', and the Earl of Pembroke 'Joseph the Jew'. In 1311, the barons forced Edward to accept the Ordinances, banishing Gaveston on pain of excommunication.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MURDER OF GAVESTON AT BLACKLOW HILL: JUNE 1312
When King Edward recklessly recalled Gaveston from exile for a third time in late 1311, civil war erupted. Trapped in Scarborough Castle by baronial forces, Gaveston surrendered to the moderate Earl of Pembroke on the solemn chivalric promise that his life would be spared while negotiations were held. However, while resting at a village rectory in Oxfordshire, Gaveston was kidnapped by the brutal Earl of Warwick, who dragged the Gascon favorite in chains to Warwick Castle. On June 19, 1312, on Blacklow Hill on the road to Kenilworth, before the eyes of the Earl of Lancaster and the rebel magnates, Piers Gaveston was run through with two broadswords and his head was severed from his body on the grass. King Edward wept hysterically upon learning of his lover's death, swearing an unyielding oath that he would never rest until he had exacted bloody vengeance upon the murderers of Piers Gaveston.  Edward's reckless decision to recall Gaveston from exile in 1312 triggered open civil war: baronial forces besieged Gaveston in Scarborough Castle, where Gaveston surrendered to the moderate Earl of Pembroke under a solemn chivalric oath that his life would be protected. But while resting at Deddington in Oxfordshire, Gaveston was kidnapped at dawn by the Earl of Warwick, known as 'the Black Dog of Arden'. Dragged to Warwick Castle and paraded before Lancaster, Arundel, and Hereford, Gaveston was taken to Blacklow Hill on June 19, 1312, run through the belly with a broadsword, and his head chopped off on the turf. When Edward learned that his beloved favorite had been butchered like a dog, he fell into hysterical weeping, swearing an unshakeable oath that he would have the heads of Lancaster and Warwick on spikes.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CATASTROPHE OF BANNOCKBURN: JUNE 23–24, 1314
While Edward was paralyzed by baronial feuds in London, King Robert the Bruce was systematically liberating Scotland, capturing English-held castles one by one until only the mighty fortress of Stirling Castle remained. In June 1314, Edward mobilized the largest English invasion army of the century—over twenty thousand veteran cavalry, Welsh archers, and heavy infantry—marching north to relieve Stirling. On June 23 and 24, outside Stirling at the Bannockburn marsh, Bruce deployed his disciplined Scottish schiltrons—dense, bristling hedgehogs of fourteen-foot spears. Edward's tactical generalship was disastrous: he crammed his heavy cavalry into a narrow, waterlogged gorge between the streams, where English knights were slaughtered in the mud, unable to maneuver. It was the greatest military humiliation in English history: Edward fled the field at a gallop to Dunbar, his army routed, leaving Scotland free and independent.  The Battle of Bannockburn on June 23 and 24, 1314, was the greatest military disaster in English history: King Edward led a colossal invasion army of over twenty-five thousand veteran knights, Welsh archers, and men-at-arms to relieve the besieged garrison of Stirling Castle. King Robert the Bruce, commanding a smaller Scottish army of six thousand spearmen, deployed his dense, hedgehog-like schiltrons on the firm ground bordering the waterlogged Bannockburn marsh. Edward's generalship was disastrously incompetent: he crammed his heavy cavalry into a narrow bottleneck between the streams, where English knights were slaughtered in the mud by bristling Scottish spears, unable to charge or retreat. King Edward fled the field at a desperate gallop to Dunbar, leaving thousands of dead knights and the entire English royal baggage train to the triumphant Scots.

ACT V: THE TYRANNY OF THE DESPENSERS AND LANCASTER'S FALL: 1318 TO 1322
Following the disaster of Bannockburn and the Great Famine of 1315 that starved thousands of English peasants, Edward found a new and far more dangerous favorite: Hugh Despenser the Younger, an ambitious, greedy, and ruthless Marcher lord, alongside his cunning father. Despenser dominated the king's affection and bedchamber, using royal patronage to illegally seize vast estates in South Wales and extort wealth from rival nobles. When the Earl of Lancaster led another baronial rebellion in 1322, Edward surprised his enemies with ferocious military energy: defeating Lancaster at the Battle of Boroughbridge, Edward had his royal cousin beheaded on a hill outside Pontefract Castle, exulting in the vengeance he had promised for Gaveston a decade earlier. For four years, Edward and the Despensers ruled as unchecked, venal tyrants, executing opponents and confiscating lands.  In the wake of Bannockburn and the horrifying Great Famine of 1315 that left English peasants eating horses and dogs, Edward found a new and far more sinister favorite: Hugh Despenser the Younger, an arrogant, corrupt, and insatiably greedy Marcher lord who completely dominated the king's bedchamber and government. The Despensers used royal writs and forged deeds to violently seize lands across South Wales, alienating the entire aristocracy. When Thomas of Lancaster led another baronial rebellion in 1322, Edward surprised his enemies with ferocious military energy: defeating Lancaster at Boroughbridge, Edward had his royal cousin beheaded on a hill outside Pontefract Castle, exulting in the vengeance he had promised for Gaveston a decade earlier, inaugurating four years of unchecked tyranny.

ACT VI: THE SHE-WOLF OF FRANCE AND THE INVASION OF 1326
Edward's downfall was orchestrated by the woman he had neglected and humiliated for twenty years: his queen, Isabella of France. In 1325, Edward dispatched Isabella to Paris to negotiate a peace treaty with her brother King Charles IV. Once in France, Isabella refused to return to England as long as the Despensers held power. Joining forces with an exiled English rebel baron named Roger Mortimer, Isabella took Mortimer as her passionate lover, forming an audacious alliance. At the court of Hainault, Isabella betrothed her fourteen-year-old son Prince Edward to Philippa of Hainault in exchange for an invasion fleet of eight war transports. In September 1326, Isabella—christened by history as 'The She-Wolf of France'—landed on the coast of Suffolk. The English nobility and citizens of London deserted King Edward en masse, flocking to the Queen's banner. Edward and the Despensers fled into the mountains of Wales, where they were captured in the November rains.  The catalyst of Edward's destruction was his estranged queen, Isabella of France: dispatching Isabella to Paris in 1325 to negotiate a peace treaty with her brother King Charles IV, Edward walked into a fatal diplomatic trap. In Paris, Isabella openly allied with the exiled English rebel baron Roger Mortimer, taking Mortimer as her lover and declaring that she would never return to England until the Despensers were destroyed. Landing on the coast of Suffolk in September 1326 with a mercenary fleet, Isabella—hailed as the 'She-Wolf of France'—was welcomed by the English nobility and citizens of London as a deliverer. Edward and the Despensers fled into the mountains of Wales, where Hugh Despenser was captured, hanged on a fifty-foot gallows, drawn, and quartered, while the broken king was taken in chains to Kenilworth Castle.

ACT VII: THE DEPOSITION AND THE DARK SECRET OF BERKELEY CASTLE: 1327
In January 1327, in an unprecedented constitutional event, Parliament assembled at Westminster: declaring King Edward II incompetent, tyrannical, and ruled by evil counselors, Parliament formally deposed the anointed sovereign, proclaiming his fourteen-year-old son King Edward III. Broken and weeping in black robes at Kenilworth Castle, Edward II surrendered his crown and scepter to a parliamentary delegation. Imprisoned in the dark, damp dungeon of Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire under the brutal custody of Sir John Maltravers and Thomas Gurney, Edward was subjected to systematic psychological torture. On the night of September 21, 1327, terrifying, piercing shrieks were heard echoing from the castle towers across the village of Berkeley: chroniclers recorded that the fallen king was murdered with sadistic brutality, a red-hot plumber's iron thrust into his bowels through a hollow horn to leave no outward marks of violence upon his corpse. Buried at Gloucester Cathedral, King Edward II remains one of history's most tragic figures: a gentle, artistic soul trapped in the brutal armor of a medieval warrior-king, destroyed by the unforgiving demands of power.  In January 1327, Parliament took the unprecedented, revolutionary step of declaring King Edward II deposed from the throne for incompetence, tyranny, and breaking his coronation oath, proclaiming his fourteen-year-old son King Edward III. Broken and weeping in black robes, Edward surrendered the crown and scepter. Imprisoned in the dark, damp dungeon of Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire under the custody of Sir John Maltravers, Edward was subjected to psychological torture, housed above a pit of rotting animal carcasses. On the night of September 21, 1327, horrifying, blood-curdling screams were heard echoing across the village of Berkeley: chroniclers recorded that the fallen king was murdered with sadistic cruelty, a red-hot iron thrust through a hollow horn into his bowels to leave no outward marks of violence. Buried at Gloucester Cathedral, King Edward II remains one of history's most tragic sovereigns: a gentle soul who lacked the iron armor required to rule medieval England.

CONCLUSION
